C11 (C standard revision) - Wikipedia The C11 standard introduced features like alignment specification, multithreading, and more to the C language. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/C11_(C_standard_revision) Continuing from the last series Standard features of C99, let’s continue exploring new features in the C11.
Changes from C99 # Alignment specification # The Components # _Alignas: A specifier used to force a variable or struct member to a specific byte boundary. _Alignof: An operator that returns the alignment requirement of a specific type (similar to sizeof). aligned_alloc: A standard library function for dynamically allocating memory on a specific alignment boundary. Important Rules to Remember # Powers of Two Only: Valid alignment requirements are always powers of two (1, 2, 4, 8, 16, 32, 64, etc.). You cannot request a 3-byte or 5-byte alignment. Size Multiples: When using aligned_alloc(alignment, size), the size parameter must be a mathematical multiple of the alignment parameter. If you ask for a 64-byte alignment, your size must be 64, 128, 192, etc. If it isn’t, the function’s behavior is undefined (it will often just return NULL). Standard Freeing: You do not need a special “aligned free” function in C11. Pointers generated by aligned_alloc are perfectly safe to pass into the standard free() function. Example # #include <stdio.h> #include <stdlib.h> #include <stdint.h> #include <stdalign.h> // Provides 'alignas' and 'alignof' macros // Using alignas on a struct member to force the whole struct's alignment // 64 bytes is a common size for modern CPU cache lines. struct CacheLineData { alignas(64) int data[4]; }; int main(void) { // --- 1. alignof operator --- // Checks the default or forced alignment of types printf("Standard char alignment: %zu byte
", alignof(char)); printf("CacheLineData struct alignment: %zu bytes
", alignof(struct CacheLineData)); // --- 2. alignas specifier --- // Forcing a standard char array (normally 1-byte aligned) // to sit on a 32-byte boundary in memory. alignas(32) char buffer[128]; printf("Custom local buffer alignment: %zu bytes
", alignof(buffer)); // --- 3. aligned_alloc function --- // Usage: aligned_alloc(alignment, size) // CRITICAL RULE: 'size' MUST be an integral multiple of 'alignment' size_t align = 64; size_t size = 256; // 256 is exactly 4 times 64 void *ptr = aligned_alloc(align, size); if (ptr != NULL) { printf("
Dynamically allocated memory address: %p
", ptr); // Verify the mathematical alignment by casting to an integer type if (((uintptr_t)ptr % align) == 0) { printf("Success: The pointer is perfectly aligned to a %zu-byte boundary!
", align); } // Memory allocated with aligned_alloc is freed normally with free() free(ptr); } else { printf("Memory allocation failed.
"); } return 0; } aligned_alloc is implemented by the standard memory allocator (ptmalloc, jemalloc, or tcmalloc) Kernel Internal Alignment # #define __aligned(x) __attribute__((__aligned__(x))) // Example usage in the kernel: struct network_data { int packet_count; char buffer[256] __aligned(64); }; attribute((aligned(x))) is a compiler directive not standard c only works on compilers that support GNU syntax (e.g. GCC, Clang) Sad Sad Macros # #if defined(__GNUC__) || defined(__clang__) #define MY_ALIGN(x) __attribute__((aligned(x))) #elif defined(_MSC_VER) || __STDC_VERSION__ >= 201112L #define MY_ALIGN(x) _Alignas(x) #else #define MY_ALIGN(x) // Fallback for old/unknown compilers #endif _Noreturn / <stdnoreturn.h> # Not for void. But for function that would exit in the middle or exec or somethiing equivalent.
Dead Code Elimination: It knows that any code written immediately after the function call is unreachable and can be removed from the binary. Suppressing Warnings: If a function is supposed to return an int but ends by calling a _Noreturn function, the compiler won’t complain about a “missing return statement.” Stack Optimization: The compiler doesn’t need to save the return address or preserve certain registers because it knows the “back button” will never be pressed. Example # #include <stdio.h> #include <stdlib.h> #include <stdnoreturn.h> // Defines 'noreturn' as '_Noreturn' // This function will either exit the program or loop forever. // It never hands control back to main(). noreturn void stop_everything(const char *msg) { fprintf(stderr, "Fatal: %s
", msg); exit(1); } int main(void) { printf("Initializing system...
"); int critical_error = 1; if (critical_error) { stop_everything("Hardware failure detected."); // The compiler knows this part of the code is "dead." // Most compilers will give you a warning: "code will never be executed" printf("This line will never, ever run.
"); } return 0; } Common Use Cases # Exit Wrappers: Functions that call exit(), abort(), or quick_exit(). Infinite Loops: In embedded systems, the main function or the “idle task” often never returns. Long Jumps: Functions that use longjmp() to jump to a different point in the program’s execution without returning through the normal stack. C23 - bracket syntax # #include <stdio.h> #include <stdlib.h> // C23 Style: The attribute is placed before the function declaration. // It clearly signals to the compiler: "This execution path ends here." [[noreturn]] void emergency_shutdown(const char *reason) { printf("SHUTDOWN: %s
", reason); // In a kernel or embedded system, this might be an infinite loop // or a call to a hardware reset. exit(EXIT_FAILURE); } int main(void) { printf("System heartbeat: OK
"); int critical_failure = 1; if (critical_failure) { emergency_shutdown("Power surge detected."); // This is formally "unreachable code." // Modern compilers will often omit this from the compiled binary entirely. printf("Trying to recover..."); } return 0; } Disassembly # 11fc:	48 8d 05 45 0e 00 00 lea 0xe45(%rip),%rax # 2048 <_IO_stdin_used+0x48> 1203:	48 89 c7 mov %rax,%rdi 1206:	e8 65 fe ff ff call 1070 <puts@plt> If you disassemble both executable, you can see that these three instructions are optimized in the noreturn version _Generic # Replaces stupid tgmath like generics.
//_Generic ( controlling-expression , association-list ) _Generic((variable), type1: outcome1, type2: outcome2, default: default_outcome ) much cleaner Example # #include <stdio.h> #include <math.h> #include <stdlib.h> // _Generic selects the function name (pointer), and THEN we invoke it with (X) #define absolute_value(X) _Generic((X), \ int: abs, \ float: fabsf, \ double: fabs, \ long double: fabsl, \ default: fabs \ )(X) int main(void) { int i = -10; float f = -3.14f; double d = -9.81; // The compiler expands absolute_value(d) to: // (fabs)(d) // Which is perfectly valid and causes no type conflicts in unselected branches! printf("Integer: %d
", absolute_value(i)); printf("Float: %f
", absolute_value(f)); printf("Double: %f
", absolute_value(d)); return 0; } Multi-threading support # Core components # <threads.h>: The main header. It provides the thread_local macro (a cleaner wrapper for _Thread_local), thread creation (thrd_create), and Mutexes (mtx_t). thread_local: A storage-class specifier. If you declare a global or static variable as thread_local, each thread gets its own independent copy of that variable. <stdatomic.h>: Provides lock-free atomic types (like atomic_int). These allow multiple threads to read and write to the same variable safely without the heavy performance cost of locking a mutex. Threads.h isn’t used often. Pthread in linux and WIN32 API still dominates multi-threading in C.
_Atomic uses TAS and CAS to do atomic operation without holding mutex if _Atomic is set on a lage data it might use mutex internally as a fall back Why _Atomic is superior to a manual Mutex # Optimization: The compiler can often use “Compare-and-Swap” (CAS) loops which are significantly faster than a kernel-level mutex. Memory Ordering: C11 atomics allow you to specify Memory Barriers (like memory_order_acquire or memory_order_release). This tells the CPU exactly how to synchronize cache across cores without stopping the world. Correctness: It’s impossible to “forget” to unlock an _Atomic variable. The synchronization is tied to the variable itself, not the code logic around it. Example # #include <stdio.h> #include <stdlib.h> #include <threads.h> // C11 Threads, Mutexes, and thread_local #include <stdatomic.h> // C11 Atomics #define NUM_THREADS 5 #define ITERATIONS 10000 // --- Global Variables --- // 1. Mutex-protected shared variable mtx_t shared_mutex; int shared_counter = 0; // 2. Atomic lock-free shared variable atomic_int atomic_counter = 0; // 3. Thread-local variable (each thread gets its own initialized to 0) thread_local int local_counter = 0; // --- The Thread Function --- // Must return int and take a void* argument int worker_thread(void *arg) { int thread_id = *(int*)arg; for (int i = 0; i < ITERATIONS; i++) { // --- Mutex Protected --- mtx_lock(&shared_mutex); shared_counter++; mtx_unlock(&shared_mutex); // --- Atomic Protected --- // atomic_counter++ safely increments without a mutex lock atomic_counter++; // --- Thread Local --- // Completely safe to modify without locks; no other thread can see this. local_counter++; } printf("Thread %d finished. Its local_counter is: %d
", thread_id, local_counter); return thrd_success; } int main(void) { thrd_t threads[NUM_THREADS]; int thread_ids[NUM_THREADS]; // Initialize the mutex (mtx_plain means a standard, non-recursive mutex) if (mtx_init(&shared_mutex, mtx_plain) != thrd_success) { fprintf(stderr, "Failed to initialize mutex.
"); return 1; } // Create the threads printf("Starting %d threads...

", NUM_THREADS); for (int i = 0; i < NUM_THREADS; i++) { thread_ids[i] = i + 1; if (thrd_create(&threads[i], worker_thread, &thread_ids[i]) != thrd_success) { fprintf(stderr, "Failed to create thread %d.
", i); return 1; } } // Wait for all threads to finish (Join them) for (int i = 0; i < NUM_THREADS; i++) { thrd_join(threads[i], NULL); } // Clean up mtx_destroy(&shared_mutex); // Print final results printf("
--- Final Results ---
"); printf("Expected total for shared counters: %d
", NUM_THREADS * ITERATIONS); printf("Mutex shared_counter: %d
", shared_counter); printf("Atomic atomic_counter: %d
", atomic_counter); return 0; } Subnormal floating-point numbers # Needed to represent a number smaller than the minimum of double.
If a computer needs to represent number smaller than 1.17e-38 it would just under flow to 0 and would cause mathematical errors in physics and engineering simulations It uses Subnormal Numbers to achieve this Instead of holding 1.xxxx * 2^exponenet, uses 0.xxxx * 2^minimum exponent are called subnormal numbers or denormalized numbers It has always been there but before C11, a C programmer had no standard way to know if the computer running the code would do the calculation or round down C11 simply added the FLT_HAS_SUBNORM macro so your code could ask the compiler. #include <stdio.h> #include <float.h> int main(void) { printf("--- Subnormal Support ---
"); printf("Does float support subnormals? %d
", FLT_HAS_SUBNORM); printf("Does double support subnormals? %d
", DBL_HAS_SUBNORM); // The smallest normal float vs the smallest subnormal float printf("
Smallest normal float: %e
", FLT_MIN); printf("Smallest subnormal float: %e
", FLT_TRUE_MIN); // Added in C11! printf("
--- Serialization Digits (Float) ---
"); printf("Trustworthy digits (FLT_DIG): %d
", FLT_DIG); printf("Round-trip digits (FLT_DECIMAL_DIG): %d
", FLT_DECIMAL_DIG); // Demonstration of the Round-Trip problem float original = 0.1f; // If we only print to FLT_DIG (6 digits)... printf("
Printed with %%..%df: %.*f
", FLT_DIG, FLT_DIG, original); // To guarantee another parser rebuilds the EXACT binary representation of 0.1f, // we must print using FLT_DECIMAL_DIG (9 digits). printf("Printed with %%..%df: %.*f
", FLT_DECIMAL_DIG, FLT_DECIMAL_DIG, original); return 0; } Macro Type Example What it tells you Trustable Digits FLT_DIG (6) Decimal -> Float -> Decimal. How many digits you can parse without the math getting fuzzy. Round-Trip Digits FLT_DECIMAL_DIG (9) Float -> Decimal -> Float. How many digits you must print to serialize a float perfectly. Subnormal Minimum FLT_TRUE_MIN The absolute smallest non-zero number possible, including denormalized states (C11). Anonymous Unions and Structs Inside Struct # Pre C11 # #include <stdio.h> // Pre-C11 Style struct LegacyVector { union { struct { float x, y, z; } coords; // Named struct float array[3]; } data; // Named union }; int main(void) { struct LegacyVector v; // Look at this terrible, verbose syntax: v.data.coords.x = 1.0f; v.data.coords.y = 2.0f; v.data.coords.z = 3.0f; printf("Legacy X: %f
", v.data.coords.x); printf("Legacy Array[0]: %f
", v.data.array[0]); return 0; } C11 # #include <stdio.h> // C11 Style struct ModernVector { union { // <-- Anonymous Union struct { float x, y, z; }; // <-- Anonymous Struct float array[3]; }; }; int main(void) { struct ModernVector v; // Beautiful, clean access. // We are writing to the exact same memory location... v.x = 1.0f; v.y = 2.0f; v.z = 3.0f; // ...but we can read it directly as an array without deep nesting! for (int i = 0; i < 3; i++) { printf("Index %d: %f
", i, v.array[i]); } return 0; } Just like thread macros, MSVC and GCC had supported anonymous structs and unions as non-standard compiler extensions before C11 Static_assert # #include <stdio.h> #include <assert.h> // Provides the static_assert macro // Guarantee that we are compiling on a 64-bit system where pointers are 8 bytes. static_assert(sizeof(void *) == 8, "This code requires a 64-bit architecture!"); // Guarantee that an integer is exactly 32 bits (4 bytes). static_assert(sizeof(int) == 4, "Integers must be exactly 32 bits."); int main(void) { printf("Architecture checks passed! Compiling...
"); return 0; } Exclusive create-and-open mode for fopen # #include <stdio.h> #include <stdlib.h> int main(void) { const char *lock_file = "app.lock"; // Attempt to open the file in exclusive mode. // "wx" guarantees that if "app.lock" already exists, this fails safely. FILE *fp = fopen(lock_file, "wx"); if (fp == NULL) { fprintf(stderr, "ERROR: Another instance is already running " "(or lock file '%s' exists).
", lock_file); return EXIT_FAILURE; } printf("Lock file acquired. Running application...
"); // Write our Process ID (PID) to the lock file just as a best practice fprintf(fp, "LOCKED
"); // Do the actual application work here... // Clean up fclose(fp); // Remove the lock file when the program finishes normally if (remove(lock_file) == 0) { printf("Lock file removed safely.
"); } else { perror("Failed to remove lock file"); } return EXIT_SUCCESS; } Behaves like O_CREAT|O_EXCL in POSIX Fixes TOCTOU Time-of-check to Time-of-use race condition Used heavily in security critical systems Still lacks permission control Linux / macOS users use open() with O_EXCL with permission bits // POSIX way: Atomic creation AND secure permissions int fd = open("lock.txt", O_CREAT | O_EXCL | O_WRONLY, S_IRUSR | S_IWUSR); Others # Improved Unicode support Unicode in data Removal of gets function Bounds-checking interfaces (Annex K) not widely implemented Microsoft had _s functions before C11 lacks standardization Analyzability features (Annex L) nobody adopted quick_exit timespec_get macros for complex values

C99 - Wikipedia The C99 standard introduced many features that are now standard in modern C development. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/C99 Kconfig Language — The Linux Kernel documentation Official documentation for the Kconfig language used in the Linux kernel build system. https://www.kernel.org/doc/html/latest/kbuild/kconfig-language.html Everyone thinks that they know C99 when developing in C but do they? (Well I probably don’t Xd)
Today I’ll be exploring some features of C99 to get familiar with the standard.
Features # inline # https://en.cppreference.com/c/language/inline
inline const char *saddr(void) // the inline definition for use in this file { static const char name[] = "saddr"; return name; } int compare_name(void) { return saddr() == saddr(); // unspecified behavior, one call could be external } extern const char *saddr(void); // an external definition is generated, too instead of calling the function and adding a call stack, inline keyword will hint the compiler to insert code where the function is called reducing function call overhead There is a disadvantage that the code size increases when a function is called from multiple places. I think I heard that in embedded systems, define is used instead for this reason. If you do not make it static when calling from the same file, it cannot be found. In C, functions default to extern, so there is no need to add extern when declaring them in another file. static = local Ignores inline when using -O0 To enforce inline in -O0, borrow the power of gcc attribute((always_inline)) static inline void add_one_inline(int *x) it’s better not to mess with inline unless you really know what you’re doing as compiler usually adds inline whenever applicable disassembly (AT&T) # I did not know that this was possible only after C99 😲 _Bool / stdbool.h # #include <stdio.h> #include <stdbool.h> int main() { _Bool is_today_a_good_day = 1; if (is_today_a_good_day) printf("Today is a good day :)
"); bool is_today_also_a_good_day = true; if (is_today_also_a_good_day) printf("Today is also a good day :)
"); } pretty straight forward stdbool.h # #ifndef __STDBOOL_H #define __STDBOOL_H #define __bool_true_false_are_defined 1 #if defined(__STDC_VERSION__) && __STDC_VERSION__ > 201710L /* FIXME: We should be issuing a deprecation warning here, but cannot yet due * to system headers which include this header file unconditionally. */ #elif !defined(__cplusplus) #define bool _Bool #define true 1 #define false 0 #elif defined(__GNUC__) && !defined(__STRICT_ANSI__) /* Define _Bool as a GNU extension. */ #define _Bool bool #if defined(__cplusplus) && __cplusplus < 201103L /* For C++98, define bool, false, true as a GNU extension. */ #define bool bool #define false false #define true true #endif #endif #endif /* __STDBOOL_H */ Complex type # #include <stdio.h> #include <complex.h> int main() { // 1. Declaration and Initialization // 'I' is a macro defined in complex.h representing the imaginary unit double complex z1 = 3.0 + 4.0 * I; double complex z2 = 1.0 - 2.0 * I; // 2. Native Arithmetic // You can use standard operators (+, -, *, /) directly on complex types double complex sum = z1 + z2; double complex diff = z1 - z2; double complex product = z1 * z2; // 3. Printing Complex Numbers // printf doesn't have a direct format specifier for complex numbers, // so you extract the real and imaginary parts using creal() and cimag() printf("z1 = %.1f %+.1fi
", creal(z1), cimag(z1)); printf("z2 = %.1f %+.1fi
", creal(z2), cimag(z2)); printf("
--- Results ---
"); printf("Sum = %.1f %+.1fi
", creal(sum), cimag(sum)); printf("Diff = %.1f %+.1fi
", creal(diff), cimag(diff)); printf("Product = %.1f %+.1fi
", creal(product), cimag(product)); return 0; } Flexible array members # #include <stdio.h> #include <stdlib.h> // --- Approach 1: Struct with a Pointer --- struct PointerVector { size_t length; int *data; }; // --- Approach 2: Struct with a Flexible Array --- struct FlexibleVector { size_t length; int data[]; // Flexible array must be the last member }; int main() { size_t num_items = 5; printf("=== Approach 1: Pointer Member (2 Mallocs) ===
"); // Allocation struct PointerVector *p_vec = malloc(sizeof(struct PointerVector)); if (!p_vec) return 1; p_vec->length = num_items; p_vec->data = malloc(num_items * sizeof(int)); if (!p_vec->data) { free(p_vec); return 1; } // Print sizes and memory layout printf("Reported struct size: %zu bytes
", sizeof(struct PointerVector)); printf("Struct is located at: %p
", (void*)p_vec); printf("Data is located at: %p <-- Notice the massive jump in memory!
", (void*)p_vec->data); // Cleanup (Order matters!) free(p_vec->data); free(p_vec); printf("
--------------------------------------------------

"); printf("=== Approach 2: Flexible Array (1 Malloc) ===
"); // Allocation size_t total_size = sizeof(struct FlexibleVector) + (num_items * sizeof(int)); struct FlexibleVector *f_vec = malloc(total_size); if (!f_vec) return 1; f_vec->length = num_items; // Print sizes and memory layout printf("Reported struct size: %zu bytes (Notice it's smaller!)
", sizeof(struct FlexibleVector)); printf("Struct is located at: %p
", (void*)f_vec); printf("Data is located at: %p <-- Notice it is immediately after the struct!
", (void*)f_vec->data); // Cleanup (Just one call) free(f_vec); return 0; } The 3 Golden Rules of Flexible Array Members # If you use these, the compiler expects you to follow three strict rules:
It must be last: You can only put [] on the very last variable in the struct. It cannot be alone: The struct must contain at least one other standard (named) member before the flexible array. You can’t just have a struct containing only int data[]. sizeof() ignores it: If you run sizeof(struct DynamicVector), it will return the size of the length variable (plus any padding). It calculates the size as if the flexible array does not exist at all. That is exactly why you have to manually add the array size during the malloc call. Linux Kernel Example # struct inotify_event { __s32 wd; /* watch descriptor */ __u32 mask; /* watch mask */ __u32 cookie; /* cookie to synchronize two events */ __u32 len; /* length (including nulls) of name */ char name[]; /* stub for possible name */ }; The Linux Kernel uses this technique quiet often. (At least the ones i’ve seen Xd) If name was a char * alloc struct inotify_event alloc char *name assign name to struct inotify_event Flexible Arrray Member allows alloc(sizeof(inotify_even) + /* size of name */) allocation in one go. No need to pass around pointers either It’s a neat trick!
tgmath.h # float res1 = sqrt(f); // The compiler silently translates this to sqrtf(f) double res2 = sqrt(d); // Translates to standard sqrt(d) long double res3 = sqrt(ld); // Translates to sqrtl(ld) double complex res4 = sqrt(z); // Translates to csqrt(z) printf("Float root: %.1f
", res1); printf("Double root: %.1f
", res2); printf("Long root: %.1Lf
", res3); printf("Complex root: %.1f %+.1fi
", creal(res4), cimag(res4)); compiler silently translate sqrt to sqrtf, sqrtl, csqrt don’t know if anyone uses this The ugliest C feature: <tgmath.h>
gg Designated Initializers # #include <stdio.h> struct point { int x; int y; int z; }; int main() { // Designated initializers for structures struct point p = { .y = 2, .x = 1, .z = 3 }; // Designated initializers for arrays int arr[10] = { [2] = 20, [5] = 50, [8] = 80 }; printf("Point: x=%d, y=%d, z=%d
", p.x, p.y, p.z); printf("Array elements:
"); for (int i = 0; i < 10; i++) { if (arr[i] != 0) { printf("arr[%d] = %d
", i, arr[i]); } } return 0; } Compound Literal # #include <stdio.h> struct Point { int x; int y; }; // A simple function that expects a struct void draw_point(struct Point p) { printf("Drawing at X:%d, Y:%d
", p.x, p.y); } // A function that expects a POINTER to a struct void move_point(struct Point *p, int dx, int dy) { p->x += dx; p->y += dy; printf("Moved to X:%d, Y:%d
", p->x, p->y); } int main() { // --- The Old Way (C89) --- // We have to pollute our scope with a variable we only use once struct Point temp_p = {10, 20}; draw_point(temp_p); // --- The New Way (Compound Literal) --- // We create an unnamed struct directly inside the function call! draw_point((struct Point){30, 40}); // --- The "Ultimate" Way --- // Combining compound literals WITH designated initializers draw_point((struct Point){ .y = 100, .x = 50 }); // --- The Magic Trick (Taking the address) --- // Unlike standard literals (like the number 5), compound literals actually // exist in memory. That means you can take their address using '&'! move_point(&(struct Point){1, 1}, 5, 5); // --- Array on the fly --- // We can pass an entire array without declaring a variable for it! print_sum((int[]){10, 20, 30, 40, 50}, 5); return 0; } ress using '&'! move_point(&(struct Point){1, 1}, 5, 5); return 0; } 3 Golden Rules of Compound Literals # They are L-values: Unlike a cast (e.g., (int)3.14), a compound literal actually creates a real object in RAM. This means you can get its memory address using &, modify its contents, or pass it as a pointer.
Scope applies: The temporary object is created in the scope of the block it was defined in. It will be destroyed when the block ends. Never return a pointer to a compound literal from a function!
// DANGEROUS! The array dies when the function returns. int* bad_function() { return (int[]){1, 2, 3}; } Read-only is optional: If you add the constkeyword, the compiler might optimize it by placing it in read-only memory, just like a string literal.
draw_point((const struct Point){10, 20}); Variadic Macros # #include <stdio.h> // The '...' means this macro accepts extra arguments. // __VA_ARGS__ is replaced by whatever those extra arguments are. #define LOG_INFO(format, ...) printf("[INFO] " format "
", __VA_ARGS__) int main() { int users = 5; char *system = "Database"; // Expands to: printf("[INFO] " "System %s has %d users." "
", system, users) LOG_INFO("System %s has %d users.", system, users); return 0; } This is used often in the kernel restrict keyword # This is one of the first keyword I’ve faced during my journey in 42seoul.
#include <string.h> void *memcpy(size_t n; void dest[restrict n], const void src[restrict n], size_t n); Since there’s pointer aliasing in C dest and src could be pointing to the overlapping memory location causing garbage value to be copied. void add_stuff(int *a, int *b, int *out) { *out = *a + 10; *out = *a + *b; } It cannot keep memory at register if memory overlaps have to re-read data on the second line restrict keyword promises that this memory will not be accessed by any other pointer for the life time of this pointer. Allows aggressive performance optimization - no need to re-read. It can loads giant chunks of memory to the cache Allows SIMD It is the programmer’s job to keep restrict qualification or else UB. Static in brackets # I’ve never seen this one for myself.
The problem - Array decay # void process_data(int data[100]) { // ... } In standard C, array size declared for the parameter of the function signature does not matter and simply decays into a int * void process_data_fast(int data[static 100]) { // ... } tells the compiler that data passed is never null and at least 100 in size // 'data' is a const pointer (you can't make it point anywhere else), // and it is restricted (no aliasing), // AND it guarantees at least 10 elements! void ultra_fast_math(int data[const restrict static 10]); apparently this is ultra fast…? Disassemble # lea rax, [rcx-4] mov r8, rax sub r8, rsi <-- Subtracting pointer addresses! cmp r8, 8 <-- Checking if they overlap by 8 bytes or less! jbe .L12 <-- If they overlap, ABORT and jump to .L12 sub rax, rdx cmp rax, 8 jbe .L12 <-- If they overlap, ABORT and jump to .L12 fast path - doesn’t overlap runtime overhead of checking overlap .L12: xor eax, eax .L9: mov r8d, DWORD PTR [rdx+rax*4] add r8d, DWORD PTR [rsi+rax*4] <-- Slow, 1-by-1 scalar addition mov DWORD PTR [rcx+rax*4], r8d add rax, 1 cmp rdi, rax jne .L9 slow path - overlaps Compiler Explorer - C (x86-64 gcc 15.2)
actual performance difference seems to be minimal? maybe things might much faster in other cases. Others # long long int - 64bit integer Variable Length Arrays (VLA) relegated support one-line comments snprintf <stdbool.h> , <complex.h>, <tgmath.h>, and <inttypes.h> IEEE 754-1985 Basically support for floating point Universal character names allow user variables to contain other characters than ascii

Hello. I am Minseo Park, an aspiring developer studying the Linux kernel. If you have any questions, please contact me via the contact information above. Thank you!
Skills # Languages: C, C++, Python, x86 Assembly (NASM), Bash Kernel & OS: Linux Kernel Development, Memory Management (mm), LKM, Xv6, Syzkaller, strace, GDB Virtualization & DevOps: Docker, Docker Compose, QEMU, VirtualBox System Programming: Socket Programming, Multi-threading (pthreads, OpenMP), Custom Malloc, IPC Architecture: x86, Computer Architecture (Pipelining, Cache), SIMD (AVX), AVR C Tools: Git, Make, GCC, Flex, Bison, Valgrind, CAN Timeline # September 2019 - December 2020: University of Waterloo - Mechatronics Engineering | Waterloo, Ontario, Canada (Dropped out) June 2021 - December 2021: Military service waiting period December 2021 - August 2022: Republic of Korea Army (Mandatory service) | Daegu, South Korea August 2023 - July 2025: 42 Seoul (Programming School) | Seoul, South Korea Korean campus of Ecole 42 July 2025 - September 2025: 42 Wolfsburg (SEA:ME) | Wolfsburg, Germany October 2025 - Present: Independent Research and Learning | Jeonju, South Korea Programs # Linux Kernel Mentorship Program (Part-time) | Remote March 2026 - August 2026 Linux Kernel Mentorship Program with Shuah Khan, a Linux Foundation Fellow and Linux kernel maintainer. Weekly office hours for guidance on kernel contributions and Q&A. Currently focusing on studying the linux-mm memory manager and bug fixing via syzbot. Personal Projects # B - Reimplemented the B language compiler in i386 (x86) assembly. Implemented a single-pass compiler using Flex and Bison LALR(1). Linux From Scratch - Built a fully customized Linux distribution from source code. Debugged boot failures using dmesg, earlyprintk, and GRUB/EFI logs. Verified kernel behavior in VirtualBox and bare-metal environments. Libasm - Coded simple functions like strlen and sorting algorithms in x86 assembly. Experimented with SIMD (Intel AVX) programming (using NASM with Intel syntax). Malloc - Implemented and explored user-level management of dynamic memory allocation. Process and Memory - Implemented and added system calls to the Linux kernel. Ft_fracol - Studied various fractal structures and visualized them using the Minilibx library. Leveraged OpenMP to parallelize serial loops and enable efficient multi-threaded execution. Little-penguine-1 - Wrote simple Linux device drivers based on the Eudyptula Challenge. Drivers_and_interrupts - Wrote a kernel-level keylogger in the form of a Loadable Kernel Module (LKM) for the Linux kernel. Webserver - Implemented a socket programming-based web server using C++. Built a parser using Recursive Descent Parsing to handle configuration files similar to Nginx. Independent Study # Operating System Engineering - Completed Xv6 kernel development labs through MIT OCW (6.1810) to simulate and debug OS architecture. Explored and implemented various OS concepts including system calls, page tables, traps, copy-on-write, network drivers, readers-writer locks, file systems, and mmap. Computer Architecture - Took Princeton University’s ELE 475 course provided by Coursera. Learned advanced topics such as pipelining, superscalar, VLIW, cache, and branch prediction. Arduino with AVR C - Explored bare-metal programming on Arduino Uno (atmega328p) using AVR C. Operating System Organization (CSE422) - Took a Washington University operating systems course that includes Linux kernel labs. The Linux Memory Manager - Detailed study of the Linux kernel memory manager based on version 6.x.
